The Real Costs of Buying
Introduction
The listed price is only the beginning. Between the down payment and the keys, a series of very real costs add up — and forgetting them is one of the main sources of stress in a first purchase.
This guide gives a full tour of the closing costs and start-up expenses, with orders of magnitude to budget well.
Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page to build YOUR complete buying budget.

The listed price is never the real cost of a purchase. This guide lists all the fees — around the transaction, the Welcome Tax, start-up, then the recurring costs — to build a complete budget with no nasty surprises.
The amounts (2026 edition) are orders of magnitude: have your specific case quantified by your notary and your broker.
The fees paid around the transaction
Listing the costs directly tied to the purchase.
Listing the costs directly tied to the purchase.
Notary fees (deed of sale, mortgage deed, verifications).
Pre-purchase inspection and, if needed, specialized expert assessments (roof, pyrite, etc.).
An up-to-date location certificate, if a new one is required (land surveyor).
Property appraisal if the lender requires it.
Adjustments: municipal/school taxes already paid by the seller, remaining heating oil, condo fees.
These amounts are generally settled at signing (except the Welcome Tax, billed later).

These fees all fall around the same time, around the transaction: plan for them in cash, on top of the down payment. A written estimate from your notary and your broker, from the start, spares you the stressful “how much do I need to bring” question the day before signing.
Emilie's tip
Ask your notary for an estimated “statement of disbursements” before signing. Seeing all the fees at once avoids the nasty surprise on the big day.
The Welcome Tax, separately
Never forgetting this item billed after the purchase.
Never forgetting this item billed after the purchase.

The transfer duties (Welcome Tax) aren't paid at the notary's: the municipality sends a separate bill, a few weeks to a few months later. On an average-priced property, this often amounts to several thousand dollars (see the dedicated guide for the calculation).

The Welcome Tax deserves a line of its own because it arrives AFTER the purchase, by municipal bill: many forget it in their budget and get caught out. Set the money aside right at the transaction — it's one of the most common cash-flow surprises for new owners.
Emilie's tip
Set the estimated Welcome Tax amount aside as soon as you sign, in a separate account. It's the classic trap: the bill arrives after the move.
Start-up expenses
Planning the cost of “taking possession”.
Planning the cost of “taking possession”.
Home insurance active from the moment you take possession.
Hook-ups and transfers (Hydro-Québec, internet, etc.).
The move (truck, movers, boxes).
Locks, first purchases (curtains, missing appliances, small jobs).
A start-up maintenance reserve (~1%/year of the value, to be set aside).

The start-up expenses (insurance, hook-ups, locks, small purchases, first jobs) add up fast in the first weeks. Plan a dedicated envelope so you don't finance your move-in on credit, at the worst moment.
Emilie's tip
Keep an emergency cushion AFTER the purchase. Many new owners reach the keys with a drained account; a surprise in the first year isn't a question of “if”, but of “when”.
Building your complete buying budget
Assembling all the items into a single figure.
Assembling all the items into a single figure.

Your total budget = down payment + closing costs (notary, inspection, adjustments, certificate) + Welcome Tax + start-up expenses + emergency cushion. It's this overall figure, and not the down payment alone, that determines whether you're really ready.
By calculating it early, you avoid the most stressful scenario: having just enough for the entry, and nothing for everything else.

Assemble it all into a single figure: down payment + closing costs + start-up + cushion. It's this total — not just the listed price or the mortgage — that determines whether you buy comfortably or tight. A complete, written budget protects you from nasty surprises.
Emilie's tip
Make your complete buying budget BEFORE shopping seriously. It's what tells you the price range you're truly comfortable in — not just your pre-approval.

Owning also means recurring costs: municipal and school taxes, insurance, energy, maintenance, condo fees where applicable. A purchase that's “affordable” at the entry can become heavy if these monthly costs are underestimated: calculate them before committing.
Emilie's tip
Add up all the real monthly costs, not just the mortgage, before committing. It's that total that will determine whether you live comfortably or tight in your new property.
